About Yi Kai
Chinese - American Contemporary Artist

In 1966, when the Cultural Revolution began, Yi Kai was eleven years old and in the fourth grade of elementary school. With schools closed, his formal education was interrupted for a year and a half. After repeating grades and completing only two years and three months of middle school, he entered the military at the age of fifteen. For a young man in China at the time, military service was regarded as both a fortunate opportunity and a respected path.

He served for nine years in the Railway Corps of the People’s Liberation Army. The early years were particularly arduous. Among his most enduring memories is being asked to draw a portrait of an eighteen-year-old fellow soldier who had died, so that the portrait could be displayed at the soldier’s memorial service the following day.

During those years, drawing was his only pleasure outside of work. With neither teachers nor art books available to him, he taught himself by closely studying the propaganda illustrations published daily in newspapers.

In 1979, through sustained effort and the generous support of those who recognized his artistic potential, he was given the opportunity to participate in the establishment of the Fine Arts Department at the PLA Academy of Arts in Beijing. He later took the national entrance examination and was admitted to the Academy with the highest score, specializing in Chinese painting. After four years of study, he graduated and remained at the Academy as a faculty member.

Two years later, he entered the graduate program in oil painting at the Central University for Nationalities, where he studied for three years. In 1988, he left military service and joined the university’s faculty.

On March 11, 1990, he arrived at San Francisco International Airport as a visiting scholar. He spoke no English and had no financial support. He began again entirely from scratch, relying on his own determination and resourcefulness. He remains profoundly grateful to the United States and to a social system that enabled him to establish an independent life within a relatively short period of time.

He was fortunate to continue his work in art and art education, building a life consistent with his ideals. Although art never made him wealthy, it enabled him to live with dignity while devoting himself to work in which he deeply believed.

His life experience, together with his longstanding engagement with history, literature, and philosophy, has led him to continually examine Chinese and American cultures in relation to one another, considering their respective strengths and limitations, achievements and failures. His artistic practice has developed in parallel with these reflections and with the questions they continue to generate.

For him, culture is a way of life created by a people over generations within a particular place and historical context. Every culture contains both what is valuable and what is flawed, and every culture possesses, to varying degrees, an instinct to exclude what lies beyond its boundaries. No matter how accomplished a culture may be, no single cultural tradition can meet the needs of humanity as a whole.

Human progress, in his view, has always depended on cultures learning from one another, absorbing the finest elements of other traditions while building upon their own strengths. Through such encounters, humanity creates new ways of life better suited to its evolving needs. These innovations may take the form of values, institutions, science, art, or countless other forms of human achievement. Together, they constitute what is commonly understood as civilization.

As an artist who has lived for more than thirty years in China and more than thirty years in the United States, he sees both a responsibility and an aspiration in his work: to bring the traditions of Chinese culture into meaningful dialogue with Western civilization and, through that encounter, to create something new.
Looking back on his decades in America, he regards them as years devoted fundamentally to this pursuit.

His artistic and cultural practice is rooted in the study of humanity’s most significant cultural achievements, ancient and modern, Eastern and Western, together with sustained reflection on the conditions of contemporary human existence. He understands this as a creative journey capable of occupying an entire lifetime. Along the way, one conviction has become increasingly clear to him: understanding ideas and concepts is far more important than the blind imitation of technique.

Over many years, he has reflected on the inheritance of several thousand years of Chinese culture and on the profound transformations China has undergone during the past century. These reflections have led him to believe that Taiwan may represent an important hope for the preservation and continued development of some of the finest elements of traditional Chinese culture.

In the nearly four decades since Chiang Ching-kuo lifted martial law and political restrictions shortly before his death, Taiwan has accomplished something remarkable in the long history of Chinese civilization: the peaceful transfer of political power without war or bloodshed. At the same time, the convergence of Chinese cultural traditions and Western civilization in Taiwan and throughout the broader Chinese-speaking world has contributed to innovations of global significance, from TSMC to the AI revolution associated with Jensen Huang and NVIDIA.
For him, these achievements lend tangible meaning and cultural confidence to the conviction held by many Taiwanese that Taiwan has become a vital bearer of traditional Chinese culture.

Among serious artists of his generation, technical training was rigorous. He received seven years of formal academic training in Chinese painting and oil painting in mainland China, followed by more than thirty years of immersion in the American art world. At this stage of his career, technique itself is no longer the central challenge. The languages, methods, and physical disciplines of painting have become deeply internalized.
Yet one conviction remains absolute for him: painting is not dead, and painting must remain rooted in the human hand.

He does not adopt artistic forms simply because they are favored by the market. Each work begins with careful thought and demands the concentration of his entire being, drawing upon decades of experience, reflection, observation, and artistic understanding.

For an artist whose work is strongly conceptual and whose ideas continually evolve through new insights, one of the most difficult questions is determining which visual language can most truthfully embody a particular subject.

With every painting, from the first stroke until the moment he considers the work complete, he deliberately leaves approximately twenty to thirty percent unresolved. In doing so, he forces himself to enter territory in which the outcome remains unknown.

The process is demanding. At times it is frustrating; at others, exhilarating. The intellectual and emotional experience of exploration, discovery, repetition, revision, and transformation has become a state of mind he seeks to enter every day.

That exploration continues to produce new possibilities. Now approaching seventy, he feels that the quality of his work continues to deepen and improve. This remains one of the greatest sources of satisfaction in his artistic life.

The subjects of his paintings emerge from close observation of social reality and the innumerable conditions of human existence, considered through philosophical reflection and from broader historical and cultural perspectives. These subjects change and deepen according to time, place, and circumstance. Some are eventually abandoned, while others continue to occupy him over many years. Such decisions are governed by thought and artistic necessity rather than by the demands of the market or commercial considerations.

For him, painting is a creative process requiring the integration of mind, intellect, body, eye, and hand. An artist’s cultivation, personality, perception, judgment, and physical ability must work together in the creation of a work. Achieving this unity, and continually deepening it, constitutes the lifelong discipline of the artist.

His art website presents works created across different periods of his life. Taken together, they offer the clearest commentary on his personal and artistic journey: what he has experienced, what he has thought, and what he has painted.
It is precisely this freedom, both of thought and of artistic expression, that has at times enabled his work to anticipate aspects of social reality before they became widely apparent.

As Stewart Turnquist, then a curator at the Minnesota Museum of American Art, observed of his work in 1999: “His paintings not only explore how Chinese and American cultures can be brought together; they also point toward how we might enter the next century.”
